newsitem.title: UK: Gold steady before OTC expiry, but turbulence seen.
newsitem.headline: Gold steady before OTC expiry, but turbulence seen.

text.p: Gold made a steady start to the week but was prepared for a turbulent ride after the expiry of over-the-counter options with a possible test of $340 support, traders said.

The quiet session saw platinum and palladium prices drift lower after steep rallies last week, although the forward market was tighter. No word has emerged over the weekend on the issue of delayed Russian shipments to key importer Japan.
Bullion fixed at $341.25 an ounce, down $1 from Friday. By 1020 GMT, spot gold was quoted at $341.25/$341.65, barely changed from New York's close of $341.90/$342.40.
"$339 will probably hold for the moment. But it will try lower levels later in the week," said one dealer. "It would be adventurous to buy the market. The best thing is to go short."
Dealers said the only thing protecting gold from a fresh thrust downwards was short covering by options players at $340. Once these expired at 1330 GMT, it would search for a new base.
The fundamental picture looked grim with the prospect of central bank sales preventing gold from gathering upside speed.
The weekend meeting of the Group of Seven produced no fresh phobias for gold, although the IMF reiterated that gold sales could be an option to fund the debt relief plan to poor nations.
But it would first tap its existing resources and bilateral contributions, which was in line with earlier statements.

"The longer we wait to sell gold, the less interest income," said Jack Boorman, director of the IMF's policy development and review department. "(But) we have not yet reached the point where that decision has to be taken," he added.
Meanwhile the dollar rushed to new strengths after benign statements from G7.
Analysts said an initial slide might take gold to $337.50 with further falls eyeing the February 12 level of $336.15, although at this stage physical demand could rescue the market.
The spotlight was mainly on palladium again on Monday as one-month lease rates soared to 17-18 percent from 15 last week.
But prices eased, with spot palladium quoted $2.55 down at $156.75 after Friday's 2-year peak of $161.50 tempted sellers.
"Palladium at $160 has been a bit of a problem. Every time it gets there, it gets sold off," said one dealer.
But uncertainty over supplies from the biggest producer Russia kept the market underpinned and a new rally was possible.
Platinum came off in tandem with palladium and was quoted at $376.25/$377.25, down $2.75. Silver was glued to its $4.72/$4.74 range although a test of $4.65 was likely if gold fell sharply.
